title: Ordering at a New York Pizzeria
subtitle: A family orders dinner — including the part visitors to the US find hardest: the tip.
description: An A2 listening and reading dialogue set in a New York pizzeria, covering ordering, asking for recommendations, paying and tipping, with useful expressions and exercises.
passage: The Bennett family — Mark, his wife Laura and their son Kevin — walk into Joe's Pizza on a cold evening. The place smells of fresh dough, and it is loud with conversation.
Server: Hi there, welcome to Joe's! Table for three?
Mark: Yes, please. We've heard a lot about this place — we'd love to try some real New York pizza.
Server: You've come to the right spot. Would you like a classic cheese pizza, or something a little more adventurous?
Laura: Let's be adventurous. What do you recommend?
Server: The pepperoni is always popular. But if you want something special, try the Sicilian with sausage and peppers. That's the one regulars keep coming back for.
Kevin: Can we get garlic knots too, Dad?
Mark: Of course we can. We're not leaving without the garlic knots.
Server: Great. One large Sicilian with sausage and peppers, and an order of garlic knots. Anything to drink?
Mark: Three waters, please.
Laura: And a soda for Kevin, if that's all right.
Server: Sure. We have Coke, Sprite or Fanta.
Kevin: Fanta, please.
Server: You got it. I'll bring the drinks right out.
Forty minutes later, the pizza is gone and the server brings the check.
Server: Here you go. That comes to twenty-six fifty, whenever you're ready.
Mark: Thanks. Here's thirty-two — keep the change.
Server: Thank you very much! Have a good night, and come see us again.

Outside, Laura asks Mark why he left five and a half dollars on a twenty-six dollar meal. In the United States, she explains, servers are usually paid a low base wage and depend on tips. Leaving about eighteen to twenty percent at a sit-down restaurant is normal, and leaving nothing would be a real insult. Mark had left just over twenty percent.
"So it's not really optional," Kevin says.
"Not at a place like this," his mother says. "It's part of the price."

exercises.title: Understanding the Dialogue
exercises.instructions: The questions use different words from the text. Think about the meaning, not the exact wording.

items.prompt: The server names two pizzas she likes. Which one does she describe as the favorite of her regular customers?
items.explanation: The pepperoni “is always popular”, but the Sicilian with sausage and peppers is “the one regulars keep coming back for”.

items.prompt: Whose idea was it to order garlic knots?
items.explanation: “Can we get garlic knots too, Dad?” asks Kevin.

items.prompt: One person at the table does not drink water. What does that person have?
items.explanation: Laura asks for a soda for Kevin, and from the three choices Kevin says, “Fanta, please.”

items.prompt: How much did the food itself cost, before the extra money Mark left?
items.explanation: “That comes to twenty-six fifty.” The $32 was what Mark handed over, and $5.50 was the difference he left behind.

items.prompt: Mark pays more than the check asks for. Why?
options: Servers there earn a low wage and depend on tips
He wanted to pay for the garlic knots separately
He had misread the amount on the check
items.explanation: “Servers are usually paid a low base wage and depend on tips,” Laura explains, “and leaving nothing would be a real insult.”

items.prompt: At a restaurant like this one, how much do most Americans add to the bill?
items.explanation: “Leaving about eighteen to twenty percent at a sit-down restaurant is normal” — twenty percent is a fifth. Mark left just over that.

items.prompt: Mark says “keep the change”. What is he telling the server?
options: Do not bring the difference back — it is yours
Please bring my money back to me
I would like the bill in smaller notes
items.explanation: He hands over $32 for a $26.50 meal, and the $5.50 difference is meant as the tip.

exercises.title: Useful Restaurant Expressions
exercises.instructions: Choose the expression that fits the situation.

items.prompt: You want the server's opinion about what to order. You say:
items.explanation: "What do you recommend?" asks for a suggestion — exactly what Laura says.

items.prompt: You are ready to pay. You ask for:
items.explanation: In American English you ask for the check. (British English: the bill.)

items.prompt: The server has understood your order and says:
items.explanation: "You got it" is a fixed informal expression meaning "yes, certainly".

items.prompt: A customer who eats at the same place every week is:
items.explanation: A regular is a frequent customer.

items.prompt: You want a sweet fizzy drink in the US. You ask for:
items.explanation: American English uses 'soda' (or in some regions 'pop'); 'fizzy drink' is British.

exercises.title: Complete the Conversation
exercises.instructions: Choose the missing word in each line.

items.prompt: Server: Welcome to Joe's! ___ for three?
items.explanation: "Table for three?" is how a server asks how many people are in your party.

items.prompt: Mark: We'd ___ to try some real New York pizza.
items.explanation: "We'd love to…" is a natural, enthusiastic way to say what you want.
After taking the food order, the server asks about drinks.
The change is the money left over; telling the server to keep it makes it the tip.

items.prompt: Server: Have a good night, and come ___ us again.
items.explanation: "Come see us again" is a warm, very common American way to invite someone back.

discussion: How does tipping work where you live? Is it expected, optional, or unusual?
Role-play this scene with a partner: one of you is the server, the other orders a meal, asks for a recommendation, and pays.
Kevin says tipping is "not really optional". Do you think a tip should be part of the price instead? Why?
Write a short dialogue (about 8 lines) in which you order food and ask two questions about the menu.
